speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two questions I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance. The first arises out of a telegram I have received from the secretary of local 1064, steel workers, Sydney, Nova Scotia, setting out that men employed by the steel company and owing 1941 income tax who have volunteered for service in the armed forces were informed on applying for their wages, totalling $67, that income tax laws compelled the company to keep all their wages, since they owed more than this amount on the 1941 tax. Is the minister in a position to inform the house whether this is in accordance with government instructions to the employers?
The second question arises out of a telegram received from the president of district No. 26, United Mine Workers of America, setting out that a serious shortage of essential foodstuffs in the coal mining areas of Nova Scotia is now interfering and will in the future seriously interfere with production. Can the minister inform the house whether the wartime prices and trade board are considering this matter, and if so, what steps are being taken to improve the situation?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS FEOM PAY OP ENLISTED WORKERS-FOOD SHORTAGES
speechtext: The first question has some degree of urgency and might be asked on the orders of the day, but the second question was certainly not in that category. If the minister wishes to reply he may do so, but I submit that it is not a question that should be asked on the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA-INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS FEOM PAY OP ENLISTED WORKERS-FOOD SHORTAGES
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to send me notice of his first question. While I have not had time to secure details of the cases to which he referred, I would say that under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act, when a taxpayer is indebted to the crown, a notice may be served on any person who is indebted to that taxpayer requiring him to withhold the whole or part of the debt owing to the taxpayer and pay it over to the Receiver General of Canada. If the taxpayer wishes to have the order withdrawn he can apply to the local inspector of income tax and make arrangements to pay either by instalments or some other basis satisfactory to both the taxpayer and the department. The income tax department is 
always willing and anxious to cooperate with taxpayers and to have outstanding taxes settled on some mutually satisfactory basis of payment.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I rise to a question of privilege. On the editorial page of the Ottawa Journal of February 27, there was an editorial entitled "Ten vacant jobs for M.P.'s", concerning the possible appointment of parliamentary assistants, and which contained the two following paragraphs:
What hopes this must stir in ambitious breasts; and what vistas it must open up of prestige and authority, and patronage influence, and nice offices with private secretaries and stenographers, and soft rugs under foot, and letters written on embossed stationery! Almost we can see Monsieur Jean-Fransois Pouliot in one of these roles: liking it so much that he would consent even to be "parliamentary assistant" to Colonel Ralston.
It is a happy prospect; even though, alas, there can be only ten, with ten times that number for whom there will be only the bitterness of disappointment. If only there were more ministers!
I deeply resent the Journal's insinuation that I would run after such a job. At the start of the war the lamented Mr. Norman Rogers offered me a more glamorous position which I could not accept-not that I would shirk a duty but simply because I have not the means to be a dollar-a-year man. I shall not keep the house any longer by giving proof of what I am saying, but I am ready to show it to anyone who comes to my office to see it. AfteT all, why should the pleasures of soft rugs under foot and embossed stationery be only for the Journal tycoons?

I am not sure that this is the occasion on which to bring up the item that I wish to bring to the attention of the committee. I would have asked the question before the orders of the day were called, while Mr. Speaker was in the chair, but I felt that some objection might be raised on the ground that the question was not of sufficient urgency. I think it comes under the head of agriculture, for this reason, that since the Debt Adjustment Act in Alberta has been declared beyond the powers of the legislature, the position of farmer debtors in the western provinces is worse than it has been at any other time during the last eight or ten years. For the last few days in Saskatoon a conference on debt adjustment has been in session with a view to arriving at some plan by which bona fide farmers in the western provinces who are unable to pay their debts may receive a measure of protection.
Under the present quota system the western farmers are unable to sell sufficient wheat or to market sufficient of their products to enable them to meet their expenses and at the same time pay their creditors. The result is that on every hand there has been an acceleration of foreclosures and cancellation proceedings. The matter should receive immediate attention, and I bring it up now to ascertain whether or not the government will at once introduce some measure of temporary protection for bona fide farmers who are desirous of paying their debts but are unable to do so by reason of the present legislation which prevents them from marketing their wheat. Something should be done by the Department of Justice to assure them of protection until such time as the quotas are increased or as legislation may be passed by this parliament.
It is not a question of the farmers wishing to evade their responsibilities. It is, however, a matter of great concern to them that at a time when they are being asked by the Department of Agriculture to expand production, foreclosures are being proceeded with. The matter particularly concerns the Minister of Agriculture, because of his desire to secure increased production in the western provinces. At the present rate of foreclosures and cancellations unless something is
done to protect bona fide farmers against actions which are the consequence of the fact that protection is no longer available, many farmers will be driven off the land before spring. I am asking the government, and particularly the Minister of Justice, whether the government will not do something at this time to put an end to what I think is a most unfair course, to stop foreclosures and cancellations against farmer debtors who are unable to pay because under the present agricultural policy they are able to market only up to a certain quota.

speechtext:
I should like to confirm what my friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) has just said. I did meet yesterday afternoon with the different leaders to talk over matters with a view to facilitating the business of this week and the weeks following. It was understood that to-day the government would ask to have two items called simply for the sake of getting two departments before the committee of the whole so that any matters related to them might be taken up later in the latter part of any week if so desired. That was the sole purpose of calling an item to-day. This intention I think was mentioned at the conclusion of yesterday's sitting. It is also correct that when I came into the house this afternoon, I was told that the hon. member for Weyburn had intended to bring up a question on the orders of the day, which I understand is the question that has since come up; but having been informed by his leader that the purpose with respect to the house being moved into supply to-day was simply one of procedure and that it was desired to get on with the reconstruction committee debate so that if possible it wmuld be concluded to-day, the hon. member postponed raising the question, on the understanding that opportunity would be afforded by a motion to resolve the house
[Mr. Ian A. Mackenzie.!
into committee of supply which would be made within the coming week. That is the position as I think my hon. friend who has just spoken also understands it.

It seems to me that we are dealing with technicalities in regard to this matter perhaps more than we should. Obviously the motion to go into supply was the point at which the hon. member for Lake Centre might properly have raised his objection to the farm adjustment act; but now that the point has been raised, since the Speaker left the Chair so very quickly, and since the hon. member was on his feet for some considerable time before even I noticed him, it 'seems to me that we might readily abandon any small technicalities that may exist and permit a discussion at this point. It was not my understanding that any objection would be taken to a point of this kind being raised at any time on going into supply, though perhaps I may have been confused in that respect. I did not anticipate that there would be a discussion on the first item of the estimates to be called; I naturally expected that the government would ask to have the item stand, but certainly it was not clear to me that there would be any objection to the hon. member for Lake Centre raising this question at any time on the motion to go into supply. Perhaps in that regard the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the Prime Minister and myself did not reach a common understanding. I should like it to be distinctly understood, however, that since the point has now been raised, and there could have been no objection on the part of the government to its being raised on going into supply, I do not think the rules should be used to prevent further discussion of the matter.

It seems to me we are now discussing two questions. The understanding I had from our meeting last night was in accordance with that expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. perhaps through a misunderstanding, and because Mr. Speaker left the Chair so quickly. We know what the privy council did in this matter. But surely under the War Measures Act, the government if it so desired could take action to prevent wholesale foreclosures and cancellations in western Canada, pending some decision being made.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The information we have is that no wholesale foreclosures are taking place in the western provinces at the present time. That is the information I have received from reliable sources in those provinces.

Mr. Chairman, the explanation given by the minister, that the ministry has not had an opportunity of examining the text of the judgment of the privy council, is not satisfactory. In July of 1942 the Supreme Court of Canada declared the debt adjustment legislation in Alberta beyond the powers of the legislature. At that time I raised the question in the house and asked the Minister of Justice whether consideration had been given to bringing in some temporary relief under the War Measures Act, the minister said consideration was being given the matter. Post-War Reconstruction

The house resumed from Monday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre) for the appointment of a select committee to study and report upon the general problems of reconstruction and reestablishment which may arise at the termination of the present war.

subsubtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night a few minutes before the house adjourned I began to discuss to some extent the speeches which had been delivered by hon. members in various parties. For a short time, if I may, I should like to continue along that line.
All hon. members of the Liberal and Progressive Conservative groups who spoke agreed that we should have free enterprise in the post-war period. My group would also agree, although I am not sure that we would accept without qualification the word "free". But we surely do believe in individual enterprise. The hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Claxton) pointed out that we had two million people to put to work in the post-war period, and four billion dollars to find and to distribute throughout Canada in order to maintain the standard of national income of eight billion dollars which we enjoy at the present time.
The questions naturally arise, how are we to find work for two million people, and how are we to find the four billion dollars to spend. No word was uttered by anyone, either Liberal or Progressive Conservative, as to how. those two questions might be answered. I am sorry the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speakers also ignored the point.

And we will be listening at the proper time. My question is, how? It seems to me if the house could agree upon defining the issues and finding where the clash arises among the schools of opinion in the house, and if we could agree to discuss that clash of opinions, we should really get a great deal farther.
I believe all of us agree-all members throughout the house-that we ought to use Canada's natural resources to the limit. Where
is the Liberal, the Progressive Conservative, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member, the social crediter, the united reformer, or any other member in the house who does not say we ought to use the resources of Canada? Why not grant that? Why discuss it at all? Surely we want the facts. Where is the Progressive Conservative who does not believe we should have reforestation in Canada? There is not one in the house. Why discuss it, then? Where is the individual who would not agree that we should have irrigation in Canada from coast [DOT]to coast, wherever irrigation schemes are feasible? Anyone would agree to that. Then why spend time discussing it? Where is the person who would not agree that we should have electrification on our farms from coast to coast? No one would dissent from that view. Where is the individual who would oppose the carrying out Of health schemes throughout Canada? No one would question the idea of free hospitalization and state medicine and every other kind Of assistance to the people that would raise th^ir standard of health. Not a soul would question that. There would be some who would ask, as soon as the question was raised, "Where is the money coming from?" But granted that the money is available, no one would doubt that we should have all desirable health measures. Then w-hy argue about them?
I think everyone agrees that housing schemes are desirable. There is not a member in this house, granted that the money is available from a suitable source, who would not advocate that everyone in Canada should live in a comfortable home. No one would question that every one of our aged people . should have a more munificent allowance than S20 per month. No member in the Liberal ranks, and I am sure no one in the Progressive-Conservative or in any other rank, does not feel aggrieved. that our aged people are condemned to the meagre allowance they now have. No one would not gladly give the old age pension at sixty-five years of age provided he knew where the money was coming from. Why spend our time discussing such matters?
I believe that there should be federal aid for education. Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) set forth the inequities in our educational system in Canada, and I believe we all heartily agree with what he said. The question that immediately comes to the mind of many is, "Where is the money to come from?" Suppose I spend a little time on that question. In addition to the question where the money is coming from is the question where markets are to be found. At the present time we are short 2,000,000 of our best effectives in Canada, and yet we are able to produce all the goods with which to supply the remainder of the Canadian people with a reasonably good standard of living in war time. We are also able to maintain these 2,000,000 at a good standard of living. At the same time we are devoting a great deal of our energies to the manufacture of munitions to be wasted. AVe are to be faced with the real difficulty of setting these 2,000,000 to work when they come to produce consumer goods, and of disposing of the goods which they will enable us to produce. I should think that that problem will be a real problem for anyone, no matter what his economic ideas may be.
So far as the Liberals are concerned, with the ideas that they express, it will be a hopeless problem. With the ideas that the Progressive Conservatives have expressed, I say again it will be a hopeless problem. What success the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation could achieve is an open question. We set forth in clear and unmistakable terms, which our friends may or may not understand, exactly what we propose.
Suppose Canada were going to use socialization as a means of solving the two problems, first, that of markets and, second, that of putting people to work. Let us suppose that socialization means government ownership. Take for example a shoe factory. A shoe factory is limited in its output by the number of shoes it can sell. At the present time there is probably a scarcity of labour, but, generally speaking, the only limit to the output would be the number of shoes that could be sold. The Canadian National Railways, which is government owned, has just as much difficulty selling tickets as the Canadian Pacific railway, which is privately owned. The mere fact that a government owns a factory, or that the people own a factory, or that a municipality owns a factory, will not enable that factory to sell its goods.

Well, I will leave someone else to fight with that particular dragon. They are talking about the destruction of the sovereign power of this government-which is undoubtedly treason or sedition.
May I turn now to the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) ? I may return after a while to the hon. member for Essex East. At page 813 of Hansard I find these statements by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George:
It is easy enough to look ahead apd see what labour wants. Labour does not want handouts; labour wants an opportunity to work. Agriculture wants an opportunity of selling its products at fair prices. Industry wants a chance to make a fair profit. It is that kind of thing wre should have in our minds to-day.
With every one of these sentiments every hon. member will agree. It is the method of achieving the objectives concerning which we shall disagree; and apparently the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George thinks we shall be able to solve all these problems if he ties enough other nations tight up to us so we cannot move. I turn to another page. He read from the Bank of Canada report a statement with which I think no one would disagree. I read from his quotation:
"If we are to maintain full employment in peace time, we must substitute other objectives for the current will to ivin the war. Broadly speaking our goals should be to provide a rising standard of living and to contribute to the establishment of a 'world economy which will remove the threat of war."
I think we all agree. Once more, it is the method of attaining that objective which we are interested in. May I read now a third excerpt? He was referring, apparently with a great deal of sympathy, to what Australia did. He says:
. . . they have already faced one part of the problem by calling together a constitutional convention in which the federal government sought for a term substantial powers from the states in order to carry out the purposes of the national government after the war. It was interesting to note that in putting this forward the attorney general of the commonwealth of Australia said that Australia was committed to a course of action under the Atlantic charter which she could not fulfil under the existing constitution. I think that should lead us to consider in Canada if it is possible for us to fulfil our obligations under the Atlantic charter and to the Canadian people under our existing constitution.
May I break in to raise this question: What can that statement possibly mean other
fMr. Martin,]
than that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is envisaging a change of the British North America Act which will take away the powers which were conferred upon the provinces by that act? I read on:
The Atlantic charter to-day constitutes a treaty for Canada. It was signed on August 14, 1941, by Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Churchill, and paragraphs 4 and 5 read-
I will omit the reading of these two paragraphs. Apparently this gentleman is in favour of using the Atlantic charter as a lever to force the Canadian people to swallow the idea of destroying the British North America Act.
May I say right here that there are two constitutions in the world which are proof against the contrivings of a group of gangsters who are trying to bring this thing about-this "united nations," this destruction of the British empire, this general enslavement of mankind. There are two constitutions which are proof against their machinations. One of them is the British North America Act, and the other is the constitution of Australia. And the gangsters have been at work industriously for several years, trying by one means and another, by fair means and foul, by all sorts of specious reasoning and persuasion and high powrer propaganda, to get the peoples of Canada and Australia to give up their constitutions. Apparently the hon. member has become imbued, let us say unconsciously, with the sentiments of the gentlemen who are seeking to destroy the constitutions of this dominion and of Australia-two of the greatest democratic constitutions on earth.

It is impossible to convince a man against his will. May I read further from the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. He said at page 815 of Hansard:
. . . and in the second place, have we contributed as much as we can to setting up the internal machinery to bring that about between nations? My suggestion is that though Canada has done much we can still do a great deal more.
I take that as another veiled reference to the destruction of provincial power within this country. No government that has ever sat in Ottawa has done so much to weaken and destroy provincial power as the government now sitting in Ottawa. The Sirois report was designed purely for that purpose -purely. What I want to know is this: If the British North America Act were destroyed, how could that possibly help us to find four billion dollars to spend in this country? How could it possibly help us to put two million people to work in this country? It could not possibly help us. So that all the efforts of those who are trying to attain these two objectives, the destruction of the British North America Act to centralize power in
Ottawa, and the destruction of the British empire by putting controlling power into the hands of some international government, will in no way help to solve the problems we have before us. They are utterly beside the point.
I should have liked to discuss the tourist trade. I commend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George for advocating an increased tourist trade. There are difficulties in the way, but I have not time to deal with them now because I have had to spend so much time in answering the questions of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards). If it were possible to solve our problems by those two devices which the Liberals are advocating, it would be quite a different matter; but it is impossible to solve them by those means, and to attempt to do so would only mean that we should lose our birthright without even getting a mess of pottage in return. The Liberals will wake up ten years from now to see what a monstrous thing they have done when somebody else is suffering the consequences.
An. hon. MEMBER: What about the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation?

The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation would be as bad as the Liberals or worse. They supported the Sirois report. That was clear evidence that they did not know what it was all about.
I turn now to the question whether the problem can be solved without resorting to these two most undesirable means of centralization. subsubtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
First I wish to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) on the speech he made on Friday last. In that speech he showed that he thoroughly understood the position of men in the air force who return to Canada or are discharged. He also included the other two branches of the armed services, but he emphasized for the most part the rehabilitation of men of the air force. The other two branches of the armed forces of course have to be included; they are all in this.
This motion is to set up a reconstruction and reestablishment committee. The committee should do everything in its power to find out just how the men who are being discharged from our armed forces, or who have been discharged in the past, can be rehabilitated. Some of these men have been discharged because they were wounded, some because, through no fault of their own, they have become physically unfit to continue. When they are discharged they may not be able to get a job in industry because their discharge paper says they are physically unfit for further active service. In many cases they cannot do a full day's work; they can do only a few hours' work a day. Employers in Canada do not want-at least some employers -to take on men who can work only a few hours a day. I do not know whether it is entirely the fault of the employers, or whether the blame should be put on the selective service. In Britain thousands of men are working only an hour a day, or two or three hours; and women also. Selective service in Canada should see to it that these men and women are employed for a few hours a day, if that is all they are able to do.
Of course there is a chance that some of these men may not fit into some jobs. If that is so, schools to teach and train them should be set up so that they will have a job not only at the present time but in the years to come after the war. I know that many of these men have received pensions. Speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I mentioned the case of a man who had a pension of forty dollars a month, but who was unsatisfied with life because he could not get anything to do. These men simply have to have something to-do to occupy their minds and help them reestablish themselves in civil life. Therefore I wish to point out to the members of the committee and to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) that the first duty of the committee is the reestablishment and rehabilitation of these men by fitting them to do something to occupy themselves-

Post-War Reconstruction
These men have given all they can for us; surely we can do something for them. We should be willing to give all we have to them; and God help Canada if we cannot look after those men now, because if we cannot, what will happen when the war is over and thousands upon thousands of them return to Canada? I have here a letter, dated February 19, which I should like to read:
Dear Gordon,
No doubt you get many sob stories through your daily mail, and here is another one. I feel that it is probably useless in writing on the matter, but I have been approached to do so, and you will pardon any intrusion.
A young lady in town whom you probably know was married in England nearly three years ago to a chap in the Canadian army. This boy served overseas for three years as quartermaster sergeant and his unit took part in the Dieppe incident. Prior to this the boys were given a rigid physical examination and he was found to be in a diabetic condition and sent home to Montreal.
He is getting a pension of $60 a month, but is most despondent, which, of course, is part of the disease, as he is unable to secure employment owing to the fact that he is unable to work full time. He has had good care in Montreal, but a full time job is definitely out.
I will say for the Minister of Pensions and National Health that he has been very generous in giving pensions to these boys. But that is not enough. Of course they have to have money, but money wull not bring happiness to them; they simply have to have something to do if they are to be reestablished in active life. Many of these boys, and women also, are only in the 'teen ages. They all have to be looked after, because they have many years ahead. They should be trained in different professions and callings. We are short of doctors, nurses, scientists. I do not see why they cannot be trained in those callings.
No doubt hon. members have noticed in the press in the last few months that county councils throughout the country and other municipal councils have been discussing reconstruction and reestablishment after the war. I have here a letter from the warden of Peterborough county which I should like to read:
At the January session of Peterborough county council a rehabilitation committee was set up with these thoughts in mind:
Better roads and bridges.
Development of roads to water for tourists.
More rural hydro.
Reforestation.
Rural housing on farms for hired help.
Better rural schools.
This is intended to create work for our returned men. What has dominion government in mind?
Will money be available for this work?
From whom can I get information?
Yours sincerely,
Peter J. Mather, Warden, Peterborough county.
He mentions roads and bridges, also roads leading to lakes; I take it he means roads that will be used by tourists coming to Canada after the war. Every hon. member will agree that after this war is over we shall simply have to start at scratch to rebuild out tourist trade, because nearly all the advertising that was done before the war is completely lost. To get these tourists to Canada we must have good roads, good accommodations, good fishing, and attractions to offer. The tourist business is very important to Canada and to the people in every section of Canada, because in many cases it means their livelihood. And this of course will help the men who return after the war. It will mean work for our people, a greater national income, and foreign exchange which we certainly need.
Last night the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) said that when this war is over the tourist business will boom. I do not agree with the hon. member. The tourist business will not boom unless we go after it. I do not think more than a very little of the tourist business we had before the war will come back to us. We shall have to go out after new prospects. Our advertising will have to cover the whole of the United States, central America and South America, and I know that when I say this, Mr. Leo Dolan, who is director of the Dominion of Canada travel service, will agree. Central and South American countries are bidding for the tourist trade of the United States, and now that the connecting links are being finished on what is called the allAmerican highway running from Alaska to South America, over fifteen thousand miles in all, the tourists of the United States will travel on that highway, which has been so well advertised. We in Canada must do our own advertising, and we -must make the Alcan highway attractive to United States tourists. In Colombia and I believe also in Mexico the governments have built inns and hotels at various points along the highway, half a day or a day's auto-run apart, and put them in charge of managers who are appointed on the understanding that if they do a good job, at the end of ten years the hotels will be turned over to them. The Alcan highway is some 1,650 miles long, I believe, and if we are to get any share of the tourist trade from the United States we must build inns and hotels on the Alcan highway and trans-Canada highway, on the same basis as they have been built in Colombia and Mexico.
The countries of central and South America, including Mexico, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Colombia, Peru, the Argentine, Chile
Post-War Reconstruction

and all the rest of them, are doing everything possible, spending many dollars, to advertise their tourist attractions. There is also a pan-American congress which meets every year to discuss the tourist business. They have much to offer, much with which to attract tourists. In Guatemala, for instance, the road is 12,500 feet in the clouds; in Chile, down below Santiago, the capital, there is an all-year highway through the lake district. They have wonderful routes and splendid scenery; in Mexico they have pyramids, ancient cities and all the rest of it, and we in this country must do something to offset those attractions. They get out booklets describing the twenty-one nations belonging to that union, with stamps showing different views in the various countries. I have been in all those countries, and I have an idea what they are going to do in an endeavour to take away our tourist trade. Therefore I urge as strongly as I can that this committee set up a tourist subcommittee to bid for the American tourist trade. We simply must have it; our country cannot live without it. I make that statement because I represent what I claim to be the best and most beautiful tourist district on the whole continent, the Kawartha lakes region, and I know what the tourist business means to our people. I know also what advertising means if you wish to get tourists, because I have been on tourist committees since 1920, and was a member of the first executive to be set up by the Ontario Tourist Association.
In my opinion the Alaska highway should be beautified, and so should our transcontinental highway. Both these routes also should be controlled, because we cannot allow them to become billboard highways, as many of our other highways have become. When you start allowing billboards to be erected along your highway, you find that they block out the very best views; therefore I sincerely hope something will be done to control billboard advertising along these roads.
In his letter the warden also mentioned the need for more rural hydro, meaning of course electric appliances in every farm home, with consequent better health. In electrifying our farms we would be helping the workers in the cities, because every electrified farm means an electric iron, an electric refrigerator, an electric washing machine, an electric milking machine and so on, all of which would mean employment to the factory worker. We must look at every angle of this question so that when our boys come home they will not have to ride the rods again as they did after the last war. We cannot allow that now. If it is possible for us to spend five and a half billion dollars-or for all I know it may be 
six billions when the minister speaks tonight-for the prosecution of the war, God help us if we cannot spend at least two and a half or three billion dollars in peace time. I know it will hurt our pockets, but if we have a happier country that will not matter.
In his letter the warden also mentioned the lack of farm housing for hired help, and I feel that he should have added better homes for the working men in our cities. I hope the committee will also consider the advisability of tearing down or moving many of the war-time houses when the war is over, because most of these houses are nothing but eyesores of the worst kind. The warden also mentions the need for better rural schools. Only yesterday I received a letter from a farmer in my riding who asked what he could do to get his two children to school, because the school, which was four and a half miles away from his farm, had been closed because there were not enough children in the district to keep it open. He felt that he might have to buy a farm near one of the other schools in order that his children might continue their education. In many rural districts you can find bright boys and girls whose education has been held back because of the fact that their fathers and mothers have not had the money to send them to high school and college. Therefore some provision should be made which would enable these boys and girls to go to collegiates and universities. This is something which has been advocated by other hon. members, and I think we should keep hammering at it until the government does something about it.
In his letter I believe the warden covered the most essential angles of reconstruction so far as the counties are concerned. The government should let the municipal bodies know what it will do in regard to funds, and give that information as soon as possible so that county councils and municipal bodies generally may make their arrangements now to set aside certain wmrks, or, as we sometimes say, "put them in the bank" until after the war.
I know these municipal bodies will see to it that for every dollar spent Canada will receive back a dollar in value.
This war is being fought for the common people. We hope the peace will be for the common people; in other words, one for all and all for one. When this war is won we must not allow the men and women of our forces to return to an unhappy Canada, a Canada in which there is no work for them. We must see that all are clothed, housed and cared for. We must have jobs for all who are able to work. It is the very least we can do; it is our duty and, may I say, our privilege.

Post-War Reconstruction
Mrs. CORA T. CASSELMAN (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, other hon. members who have, spoken have discussed the greater matters which will be considered by the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment. I should like to present a few of the smaller matters which, it seems to me, are of importance.
I believe that the brave new world which we hope to reach some day will be brought about by smaller things, that we shall arrive at our goal step by step. Therefore I offer just a few matters which the committee might consider when it deliberates in the coming weeks. We realize there is a new factor which will confront Canada and all other nations in the post-war period, in that hundreds of thousands of women will be demobilized from industry and from the armed forces at the close of the war. They are women who, to a great extent, had no previous employment beyond their own home circles. Many of them had not finished their education. Much of what the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) said last Friday with respect to the boys in the Royal Canadian Air Force applies with equal force to the girls in all branches of the armed services. They will come back, possibly not to jobs but rather to fit in some way into a civilian life.
We must have a great deal of sympathy with both the men and the girls who will come back to things much different from what they are now experiencing. They will have difficult adjustments to make. We can give them sympathy, and we may do something for them through legislation. The girls may welcome getting back to the four walls of their homes, because those home walls do not limit them now in the way in which they did a few generations ago. A woman with the ability and the desire may go far beyond those four walls, into many other spheres of activity. While they have had a greater degree of regimentation in the armed forces, yet perhaps they have also had greater independence. They have had control of their own money, little though it may be. They have had the exhilaration of being part of a great crusade. They have drunk of the heady wine of adventure, just as the boys have. So that if they have difficulty in making adjustments when they come back, we shall have to assist them in that regard. We who are older realize that their reestablishment is of great importance, both for the individual and for the nation, because no one makes a greater contribution to the life of the nation than does the woman whose career is in the home. She must have some of the noblest qualities if she is to do her work with 100 per cent efficiency. She has to bring up her
children so that they may be tolerant, broadminded, mentally alert, so that they may have a respect for the rights of others and may be good citizens in a democratic country. She must preserve the balance between freedom and discipline. Not only must she. build character in our young people, but it must be built so that that character will be maintained in the adults. Moreover, I do not think the father's place in the home is of any less importance than the mother's. Our nation's grandest qualities are built in our homes.
I believe we must consider at the present time some system of children's allowances. That would be one of the definite recommendations I would make to the committee. That is one of the provisions which should be made for the returned men and women. There is now a provision whereby for a short time after his or her discharge a member of the armed forces receives military pay. I would suggest that in post-war years that might be a longer or a more flexible period. At present the period allowed by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) may be sufficient, but during the years of adjustment after the war it might be more flexible if it were long enough to provide time for adjustment and short enough to prevent malingering-because there will be some who will take advantage of it, if they can. I believe that group, however, will be small in number when compared with the thousands who will play fair.
This would help the morale of the nation, something which will be of great importance if we are to make progress' along democratic lines. We realize that morale is a decisive factor now on the home front, and at every point where our armed services are sharing in the struggle against despotism.
Another point which might be considered by the committee is that of discharge papers for both the men and the women who will leave the army. I am wondering if we could not work out something of which they might be proud in days to come, something which would indicate what they have accomplished through their willingness to make the supreme sacrifice, .if necessary. When they volunteered to enter the armed services they showed they were willing to do what their country called upon them to do. Perhaps discharge papers should express some measure of their country's thanks, so that they may have something in which they may take pride, and which their children may cherish.
The committee will consider the larger problems, and properly so. They will no doubt discuss housing, conservation, and the use of

Post-War Reconstruction

our natural resources. I have no doubt they will discuss national parks and playgrounds, and when that subject is under consideration I wonder if they would keep in mind smaller playgrounds which would be within the daily reach of children in crowded areas in our . cities. So	many	children have	only	thestreets and	lanes	in which to	play.	Itwould be worth while to tear down some of the old decrepit buildings, or fill up the vacant lots by providing playground accommodation to	which	children could	have	easyaccess every	day of	their lives. I	know	that
matter comes under municipal jurisdiction, but it seems to me that the recommendations which will be made by the reconstruction committee will have some weight with the municipalities and they may agree to provide playgrounds for our children which will help to build character.
I consider that play is simply a younger sister of education, to which a number of hon. members have referred. If we have playgrounds it means that we must have supervision because, just as in the international field, there will be bullies and aggressors who will try to push others aside. Most youth organizations and those dealing with such matters find that training is necessary for supervisors. The Y.M.C.A., the Canadian girls in training, the boy scouts and many church organizations have tried to train people to take charge of children's groups. I suggest that we consider such training as part of the vocational training now being provided under the auspices of the dominion and the provinces in order that there may be a greater number of trained and efficient supervisors who could help these young people along. Such work might be made available for some of those discharged from the armed forces.
The children learn in the playgrounds to have respect for the rights of others while standing on their own rights. That is what we want in the international field. Perhaps this comes into federal jurisdiction because those who receive character training are less likely to become delinquents. At the present time there is a great increase in juvenile delinquency with so many fathers away, and if something could be done now to help to prevent delinquency I think we would find a great improvement. Perhaps that is in the provincial field, but many of these delinquents come back as second and third offenders when they must be dealt with under the federal system. We would be helping the nation as well as helping these young people if we could do something along these lines.
I know these are small matters in comparison with the large questions that will be before
[Mrs Casselman.]
the committee, but I think they should be kept in mind. In the olden days children were taught in the home; they came under the influence of the home, the school and the church. Nowadays there is a whole battery of influences, such as the movies, the radio, the comics and so on. If we plan deliberately through our reconstruction and rehabilitation schemes to build better character in our young people,
I know it will be to the advantage of the nation as a whole, both now and later.

subsubtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seem to be two prevalent views with regard to the problem of post-war reconstruction. There are those who believe that everything will work out all right, and that all that we shall have to do will be to trust in the government of the day and we shall receive the bountiful fruits which our plans of to-day will bring forth. There are others who are not so optimistic, who look at these post-war problems in a more realistic, and at times I might say even a pessimistic way. I am inclined to agree with some hon. members that the government should at least attempt to solve some of the problems which are facing us to-day. We should then have reason to believe that we might be able to cope with other problems when they come upon us.
I have in my hand a copy of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1944, I notice that there is a decrease of $126,000 in the item for old age pensions. Looking over other items I see that there is an increase of $54,296,231.19 provided for the payment of interest on our national debt. The total interest that must be paid in the coming year on the national debt is $198,628,033.33. In view of this, anyone who wants to convince me of the government's sincerity with regard to postwar plans will have to do more explaining than has been done, especially since they have failed to solve the problem of our aged people.
Some time ago the president of the university of New Brunswick spoke to two' hundred Y.M.C.A. delegates from the maritimes and British Columbia. The report of his speech appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 12, 1941, and it reads:
Speaking of the post-war world, Professor MacKenzie said there would be "disorganization and debts and poverty and suffering, but that is the price we pay for the luxury of war. Industry and finance and commerce and government will operate much as they have in the period just past.	_
Taxation will continue at high levels, but that in itself need not alarm us, for taxation is merely a method of transferring wealth and of making accumulations of it available for large-scale use."

Post-War Reconstruction
Of course that gentleman is looking at the whole problem of post-war reconstruction in an, extremely pessimistic way, and I am not inclined to agree with him any more than I agree with those who have expounded the view that we shall have a paradise if only we continue carrying on under the old system.
Again, here is a pamphlet which I am sure other hon. members have received also. This pamphlet contains an address delivered by Mr. Walter P. Zeller, and is entitled, "Post-War Freedom." I believe this is an address delivered before some club in Canada, although it is not stated in the pamphlet just what club it was. I should like to draw the attention of the house to what I believe to be the most important point raised in his speech. It must be remembered that Mr. Zeller is one of the leading business men in Canada; he is regarded by many industrialists as one of the leading lights in the business world. A speech made by him on post-war reconstruction should be widely read; it should also be scrutinized to see whether he has anything worth while to put before us. Discussing the post-war freedom, which we all want, Mr. Zeller, I believe, makes out a good case. None of us want any more regimentation than is absolutely necessary. But when Mr. Zeller comes to the question of finding money to finance the post-war reconstruction, this is what he says:
It is natural that people should ask why it is that government can find all the resources needed to wage war but cannot do the same in the interests of peace.
That is a good question. Let us listen to the answer.
The answer, of course, is that the problems of peace-time economics are as different from the problems of war-time economics as peace is different from war.
What an answer! The whole problem of post-war reconstruction is involved in this question, and that is the best Mr. Zeller has to say in this regard. He goes on:
In the first place, the government does not find all the money it needs to pay for the war. We are by no means on a pay-as-we-go basis. Notwithstanding the present high taxation, income is only about 50 per cent of the cost. The balance must be borrowed. The record of war-time finance is outstanding and most highly commendable, but it is based on an assumption that peace will not be too long delayed.
That statement coming from Mr. Zeller, one of our leading business men, should cause us to ponder. We have now arrived at the point where is must be the responsibility of business men as well to face some of these matters realistically, and to answer so fundamental a question in this manner is by no means reassuring evidence that our business men are 72537-534
thinking seriously of how to retain private enterprise. I am a believer in private enterprise, but I do not believe in abuses, and if Canadian business men want to save the system of private enterprise they had better analyse more seriously the problems which are now facing us, and which will confont us after the war.
I am inclined to agree with the remark of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) that if the government is seriously desirous of tackling the problems of post-war reconstruction it would be well advised to begin doing so now. For example, it should take in hand at once the solution of the old age pension problem, the problem of private debt, and other problems which have faced this country for years. All the government has done hitherto has been to postpone action from day to day and from year to year, while farmers have lost their equity in their lands and today find themselves deprived of everything.
I wish to take this opportunity to ask members of the government to answer a few questions which have puzzled me for some time. How will our national debt be paid off? It has increased steadily for years and is still on the upgrade. Here are the figures per capita for the last seven years:
1936		 $371
1937		 369
1938		 372
1939		 382
1940		 387
1941		 413
1942		 445
And it is still going up. If we are to give-, our people security with freedom the government must first explain how it intends to pay off the debt of the country and where it will get the money. Then it will have to inform us where it intends to find the money to pay old age pensions, institute housing schemes, and finance other projects which will be needed after the war.
Our problem is neither one of production or one of consumption. Our people are willing to consume more than they have had an opportunity of consuming. The problem is one of distribution, and I am unable to see how any hon. member can confuse this internal question with something which is international. As a matter of fact a number of hon. members have endeavoured to place the blame on someone outside Canada for our own failure to-distribute the goods and services which we have within our country.
I believe that both the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon) have shown their desire to tackle this problem sincerely, but wishful thinking cannot solve:
Post-War Reconstruction

our problems. Both these hon. gentlemen will have to do what the hon. gentleman who holds the purse-strings will tell them to do. We shall have to get the assurance from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that no financial restrictions shall be allowed to interfere with the solution of our post-war problems. Without such an assurance all talk of postwar reconstruction is useless; it is futile and nonsensical because it can never be realized. What is the use of talking about parks and playgrounds, about our tourist trade from the United States and what they have to say about us, if we cannot tackle the fundamental problems of our life, those of providing our people with bread, clothing, shelter and health services? Why soar into the air to discuss secondary things when we cannot tackle problems which are immediate and fundamental and must be attended to now?
It seems to me that the sponsors of postwar reconstruction plans would do hetter if they took a little advice from the people, instead of trying to force on them the plans which they themselves have hatched. Why not go to the farmers of this country and say: ""You constitute one-third of our total population; we want a brief from you. What do you want after this war? Place your problems Before us and we will see what we can do." "Why not go to our working people in every factory across this country and say to them: "Get together; call a conference to discuss your problems, and then formulate your demands into a brief and present it to us." Why not go to the business men and say: "We want you to get together. Prepare a brief setting out your views and present them to us." Go to the professional men and say the same thing to them, go to our young people-and I want to stress particularly the role which our young people should play after the war- and say: "What opportunities do you want? Present us with a brief." Then, after having gathered all these briefs and studied them you would have a point of view representative of every class and every group of people in Canada. I believe that that would' really be a democratic approach to some of these problems. As it is, agriculture has absolutely nothing to say about post-war reconstruction, and I say that with all due respect to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who is an able debater. But our farmers expect more than words.
I wish to quote a few words to show what conditions have existed in this country. Here is a clipping from an editorial which appeared in the Calgary Albertan of August S, 1938. It .says:
{Mr. Hlynka.]
A friend of the Albertan's who for obvious reasons, we believe, does not wish to be named, showed us yesterday a list of debtors and their debts that he had extracted from the records of the organization of which he is accountant. Suffice it to say that each of the farmers mentioned in that list now owes after eight to twenty years, from as much as the value of the original loan to two or three times the sum and that the accumulated interest ranges from twenty-two to two hundred and thirty-eight times the face value of the loan. The figures are almost unbelievable, but there they are.
The editorial goes on:
Unless this business of farmers' debts is tackled courageously, it is quite evident that market values, commodity prices and all the factors that are usually supposed to make for prosperity will not mean a thing worth speaking of.
That was in 1938. Yet when this question was brought up to-day by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the minister said that they had not had the time to consider the problem. I say, Mr. Speaker, that one-third of our population in Canada deserve a better break than that. As a matter of fact, if things continue as they have for a number of years now, we shall have repeated in Canada what has taken place in the United States. I have here a clipping from a United States paper dated December 9, 1936, which says: "Janitor winner in ballot race; mayor is angry." The janitor beat the mayor in the race for office. It will not be long before some of our janitors in Canada get wise to the trick and beat some of our professional politicians out of their positions.
I believe that some of these problems must be tackled now. We cannot wait. The debt problem, the problem of old age pensions and many others must be faced now, and if the government is seriously concerned it will put the necessary legislation into effect. Let me quote from an election leaflet issued in my constituency by the candidate of the Liberal party before the last election. These are some of his planks: "Agriculture-parity prices for farm products-wheat, hogs, dairy products. Pool the freight on wheat." Have we that? I quote further from the same leaflet: "Reconsider the whole freight rate structure. Lower the cost of agricultural machinery. Keep down living costs. No man to lose his equity in his land. Settle old debts fairly but finally," and so on and so forth.
I have now been a member of this house for three years, and I think it is high time that some of these things were done. It would make a good beginning to post-war reconstruction. We cannot continue as we have in the past. We must begin to solve some of these problems and get them out of the way, and the sooner the better. Of course the gov-

Post-War Reconstruction
eminent in office will get the credit that is coming to it. It is not enough to wait until public opinion forces the government to move, but that is usually the speed of most governments.
I have another clipping here from the Edmonton Journal of April 23, 1939. It is a dispatch from Clarkson, Ontario, and it reads:
"Something has to be done", Councillor Mitchell said, in calling attention to conditions in his municipality. "All we are doing is creating an army of bums. We have had about 80,000 graduated from our high schools in Ontario during the past four or five years. We send them to school to acquire that education and then they have it, what good is it?
"Year after year students graduate. Perhaps a member of parliament hands them some taffy at commencement and gives them a diploma. The day after, they have nothing. I would rather have the babies knocked on the head at birth than see them turned out to wander after teaching them to feel and suffer," he stated.
That sort of thing was happening in cities all over Canada for many years. Let me read another clipping from the Edmonton Journal of February 15, 1934, at the time our Conservative friends were holding office in this country. This was the Ottawa scale: A family of two received 7-4 cents per meal; a family of four, 5-3 cents per meal; a family of six, 4-8 cents a meal; a family of eight, 4-3 cents a meal. That is something that our Conservative friends can put in their album, because those are things that have not yet been solved, or properly tackled.
Here is something about the old age pension. This is taken from the Winnipeg Tribune of April 25, 1942:
Old Samuel couldn't stretch his $20 old age pension quite far enough this month. When he went to make some purchases at a grocery store Friday he put three items in his pocket for which he hadn't the cash.
At the paying counter the clerks noticed that his pockets bulged suspiciously. They investigated, found he had hidden a pound of butter, a tin of condensed milk, a tin of cooked meat, total value 63 cents.
At 72 Samuel is almost stone deaf, and when he was haled into court this morning couldn't hear either the theft charge read out by . . . the clerk of the court or the questions asked by the magistrate.
At length, by means of exchange of written messages, Samuel was let off on suspended sentence.
If he commits the same offence within the next two years he'll be sentenced for the old as well as the new theft. Apparently Samuel doesn't intend to do any such thing, for he left the courtroom smiling.
That is the fate of our aged people. We must tackle these problems realistically and try to get rid of some of them now, because if we do not they will pile up upon us and it may be impossible to solve all of them at the same time.
We also talk about the Beveridge report. It surprises me that hon. members spend so much time on a report prepared for Britain. Why can we not get down to business and prepare a plan of our own? Why should we always be imitators? Why not consider the problem and figure out our own solution? If we know our objective it should not be very hard for us to reach it. We have all the material resources that we need and more. All we have to do is to apply a little intelligence and get these things over to our people for their use.
We have seen in this country a creeping tendency toward dictatorial bureaucracy. Instead of the government asking the different provinces to cooperate and coordinate all our affairs and with a view to arriving at a solution, we see a strong tendency on the part of the federal government to move into provincial fields and thus reduce the provincial powers to something very local. That is a dangerous trend. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) bring out this point so clearly. The Canadian people, if they intend to wait for this govern^ ment and for various other groups to make up a plan for a democratic future for them, then they had better not wait because these individuals will not plan the future for the people of Canada. They will plan the future for themselves, to serve their own interests.
Our young people are sacrificing more than anybody else in this war. When a young man reaches eighteen years of age he may be called for military service, and when he is nineteen or twenty the same regulations apply. If these young men are intelligent enough to fight the war for us, surely they are intelligent enough to cast a vote in an election. The age qualification in our election act should be changed, so that the young boys and girls between eighteen and twenty-one years of age may be included in the voters' lists, because the future of Canada will belong to the young people. In the past some have been afraid that youth might not stand for a lot of this nonsense that we have been handing out to them. It was felt that perhaps the young people would be too impulsive and would be hard to keep under control. But, if we place our problems squarely before them and tell them "these are your problems; you are a part of this nation; let us tackle them together," they will, I am sure, cooperate in a sincere attempt to find a solution.
Our young people will have to take a lead in post-war reconstruction. I have all the respect for ripe minds and ripe age, but I am doubtful about some of these ripe things, because, no matter what it is, if it is too ripe there is danger that it may not be the very best.
Post-War Reconstruction

I should like to bring out one or two other observations at this time, and perhaps touch upon some matters that have not been dealt with as yet. The people of Canada at this time are interested more in the fruits which they will get than in the plans that are advanced by various groups. We must judge every government by the results which it gives to the people, and not by the machinery set up. The machinery of government, if it does not bring the required results, is useless, no matter how well it may look on the surface. What we want in Canada, as the hon. member for Lethbridge has so ably pointed out, better than anyone else in this house, is security with freedom. One without the other is not enough. Why should we not have both? If we continue to get results we do not want, our freedom will be endangered. If we continue to give the people of Canada the results against which they are fighting then they will take it that democracy is failing. We do not want .our people even to think that, let alone be convinced of it. We want our people to believe that democracy is the only system for Canada, that democracy must be the system ini Canada. But this democracy must give our people better results. There is no other way out. We cannot afford to let our people say, " If these are the results we have achieved under democracy, then we want none of it." We shall then find ourselves in a really dangerous situation. We must give our people the results they want.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in this house for three years, and during that time I have followed the proceedings with great interest. In the course of the debates I have listened to and understood the philosophies and policies outlined by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, though I have not agreed with them. The same applies to the policies of the new Progressive Conservative party, and also to the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen), but for three solid years I have tried to understand what the New Democracy party is trying to drive at, and I have not found out yet. I listened with the most rapt attention to the two hon. members who this afternoon expounded the theories of that party. I refer to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), who has just taken his seat. We hear all that is wrong with Canada, but we are given only a few nebulous suggestions which, when tested, just do not hold water. We hear that we have piled up a tremendous debt during this war. It is true that we have piled up a tremendous debt, but we have done a tremendous job, and I do not know how

that job could have been accomplished by any country in the world without piling up a great debt. It is all very well to expound these fancy panaceas, but it is quite a different matter when one tries to put them into practice, as Premier Aberhart of Alberta discovered much to his dismay. However, it is not my intention to criticize those who have spoken this afternoon except to ask how Canada can expect to progress after this war unless it takes its proper place among the nations of the world. How much respect will our allies of the united nations have for us if such isolationism as we have heard from those two hon. members this afternoon is preached generally in this country?

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext: The word "isolation" was never mentioned.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext:
The hon. members spoke of trading among ourselves and living to ourselves. I wonder if they have not heard of the aeroplane and how it has altered all our old ideas in regard to time and distance. I say that the future of the world is dependent upon the cooperation of all nations, and Canada can be no exception. If -we do not cooperate we are doomed to failure.
This afternoon the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) offered some very good suggestions with regard to the tourist trade. I am sure the hon. member was not serious when he said his was the finest tourist district in Canada, for everyone knows that this honour belongs to the county of Leeds. I was particularly interested last evening when the subject of the tourist trade was introduced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton). I had not realized that one of our departmentsdiad the wisdom and foresight to write Americans and anticipate their needs before they came to Canada. I refer, of course, to what was done by the wartime prices and trade board in regard to our sugar, tea and coffee ration books. I was very much impressed by the letters read by the hon. member, which had been received by the wartime prices and trade board, in appreciation of its offer to furnish these ration books to our United States friends before they came here for their visits. There is one point, however, in which I think we are rather remiss. I refer to the amount of gasoline that is allowed Americans who come to Canada for fairly long periods of time, especially those who are property owners and consequently taxpayers in this dominion. I know of several older people in my own riding who are almost obliged to take recreation in the summer time, but who will be unable to come to Canada this summer unless these restrictions are lifted to some extent. I know of one family in particular who very much resent the fact that

Post-War Reconstruction
they can get gasoline for their outboard motor, to run around the lake, but cannot get gasoline for their car. I would respectfully draw this point to the attention of both the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the oil controller. When a Canadian goes to the United States he is given an A ration coupon book which entitles him to twelve American gallons a month. I certainly think Americans who for a great many years have been in the habit of coming to Canada and who are property owners here should be given an equal amount in Canadian gallons. That will go a long way toward counteracting the bad effect the severe rationing of last summer has had upon these tourists, and I believe it would bring to Canada a great many people who now fear that if they came here they might find themselves stranded.
Now for a moment I shall be most unoriginal. I agree with millions of other Canadians and go on record as stating that I believe entirely in free enterprise. I believe that free enterprise will help to rehabilitate Canada after the war, just as free enterprise has built Canada to her present state of civilization. But in order to succeed, this free enterprise must be unshackled; the fetters of bureaucracy must be removed. By this I do not mean that I would advocate reverting to the policy of laissez-faire of the last century. Industry must be policed, just as the individual must be policed.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext: Policed, but not handcuffed.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext:
But so far as definite government planning is concerned, for every move industry is to make, I am sure it would fall down. On the other hand, if allowed to advance, as it has throughout this country, to its present state, it will not let us down.. One thing we cannot do is to let our men and women down when they return from active service after the war. I cannot visualize those men and women returning to a country swayed by the panaceas, if you like, conceived by certain theorists, or influenced by the untried policies of political opportunists.
Above all, after the war Canada will have to keep its head. We will stand to come out on the very top, if things are managed and governed correctly after the peace. On the other hand, we stand to lose everything if we attempt to experiment during the vital period of reconstruction.
I believe in free enterprise, because it is through free enterprise the British commonwealth of nations, as we know it, has developed. I believe in free enterprise, because
it is upon such free enterprise that Canada was built. I believe in free enterprise because it has given the United States the highest standard of living, the highest real wages any country has ever known. Surely we shall not throw overboard something which has meant as much to humanity as this system developed through the centuries.
During the debate we have heard a great deal that has been constructive, and especially suggestions for a definite and proper program of public works after the war. We have heard about water conservation; we have heard about irrigation; we have heard about a certain measure of reforestation. I wish to bring to the attention of the house a subject which was much in the public eye before Pearl Harbor, but about which we have not heard since that time. I refer to the development of one of the greatest national resources God ever gave a continent, namely, the development of the deep waterways on the St. Lawrence river. Had it not been for Pearl Harbor I believe that waterway might have been under construction now. However as a result of the emergencies of the war it has had to be put aside for the time being-but I trust only for the time being.
Living as I do on the banks of the St. Lawrence, and watching 240,000 cubic feet per second pass my door, I cannot help thinking of the waste of power, and the waste of navigable resources. Between the United States and Canada a deep waterway has been built from the head of lake Superior to Prescott. Then there is a bottleneck for about 130 miles. At great expense the government of Canada has made the port of Montreal one of the greatest seaports in the world. Yet we have this bottleneck of. only 130 miles separating our great fresh water inland seas from the commerce of the world. At the present time the largest boats which sail the great lakes go to Prescott and unload their grain. That grain must be transhipped from the elevator at Prescott, and through the 14-foot .canal. It is either transhipped in Montreal, or again put in storage from the small canal boats. Or, in some instances, the small canal boats will take it down from the head of the lakes. This is a most uneconomical and unreasonable situation.
If such a water system existed in Europe as exists on this North American continent it would have been developed many years ago. Even to-day countries in Europe are considering further development of their waterways. Germany recently completed the Danube-Rhine system, thereby connecting the North sea with the Black sea. Some years
Post-War Reconstruction

ago Russia built the canal which passes up the Volga river from the Caspian sea, thence over to the Don river and thence into the sea of Azov and the Black sea. But none of these canals can be compared in importance with the St. Lawrence system which, with the exception of the 14-foot canal, remains undeveloped. One of the most costly sections, I should add, has been built by the Beau-harnois Power Company, but the power has been only partly developed.
The canal has been built, and all that is necessary now to connect lake St. Francis with lake St. Louis is to erect locks adjacent to the power house. Really what remains for us to do here in Canada is to reconstruct the Lachine canal which connects the harbour of Montreal with lake St. Francis and the stretch from Cornwall to Prescott.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext: Not with lake St. Francis, but with lake St. Louis.

subsubtopic: MAKCH 2, 1943
speechtext:
Yes, with lake St. Louis. This great natural resource should not be wasted. This work would mean that many thousands of men could be employed during the period of rehabilitation, and it would mean a power development even greater than that at Boulder dam or the recent development on the Saguenay river.
With all seriousness and earnestness I ask this committee to give the fullest consideration to the development of what is the continent's greatest natural resource, the St. Lawrence deep waterway.
On motion of Mrs. Nielsen the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the financial and economic requirements of war become greater, and more exacting as the scope and thoroughness of our plans grow. This fifth war-time budget will exceed all previous standards and make provision for expenditures on a scale which it is sometimes difficult for any of us to appreciate.
IMr. Fulford.]
The task of preparing this budget has been cheered by the growing evidence that we have seized the offensive, and the power of the united nations is already striking deep into the enemy's defences. There is, too, the expectation that our own land forces will soon match the blows which our air force and navy have struck against the aggressor. But if the valour of our men and of our allies is now translating our economic and financial programme into telling blows against the axis powers, there is every reason for pressing that programme forward and none for relaxing it.
As I have said frequently, financial measures are but one of the means through which we link the whole war programme together. They are instruments and not ends in themselves. They are instruments which must be used wisely lest we frustrate our efforts now and sow the seeds of intolerable conditions later. Financial measures are one of the means through which each person has his share in this war. Taxes and loans are not exactions from the people by a government. They are weapons which the people through their elected representatives and the free methods of democracy have fashioned for their own use and their common purpose. We cannot all man guns and planes and ships; we cannot all build guns and planes and ships, but the Canadian people have shown by the reception which has been given to each succeeding wartime budget that they are ready to wield these weapons, each according to his strength and all ^gainst the people's enemies. They are ready to accept their share in each increase in the effective organization for war of which the budget is but the financial counterpart.
It is by the single purpose of the people of this country and her allies that this war will be brought to the desired end. It is by the sober, tenacious purpose of the men and women of this and other countries that a just and durable peace will be written. The proposals which I shall lay before the house tonight are the recommendations which the government makes to the elected representatives of the people of this country for improving the financial means by which each of us may throw his whole weight into this struggle-and help to make possible a world more worthy of our better selves.

The current fiscal year has been marked by the coming to fruition of all our major production programmes, and yet, as we approach our full capacity, the increase in over-all production is less marked than last year.

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
Industrial production in Canada rose from an index figure of 208 in December, 1941, to 251 in December, 1942. Such over-all figures however, conceal what has been taking place.
