maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre) for the appointment of a select committee to study and report upon the general problems of reconstruction and reestablishment which may arise at the termination of the present war.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford) : I have but a few general remarks to make this evening before the minister closes the debate upon the motion to set up a committee of this house to inquire into the problems of rehabilitation and reconstruction in the post-war period.
Without any shadow of doubt, the people of this nation will feel that it is their right to decide their own future after the winning of the victory. To-day thousands of them are fighting in every field; they are engaged in a life and death struggle, first of all, for their existence as a nation, and second, for their right to be assured of democratic progress in the future.
The democratic progress of any nation depends to a very great degree upon the will of the people for progress. It depends to a great degree upon the people's understanding of the direction which has to be taken before progress can be achieved. Canadians during the last ten years have learned much. To-day they have both the will and the understanding to go on. Personally I am of opinion that when. we as a nation are rapidly approaching the great crisis when we shall be called upon to exert every effort to win the final victory, it would be well to have had committees of this house set up-even now, at this stage in the war's progress-to try to determine some of our more immediate problems. I should like to have seen a committee of this house draw up a bill of rights for labour, for there is yet much by way of contribution which labour must make before the final victory is won. I should like to have seen the committee take upon itself the function of determining further ways and means of strengthening the relations between government and management and labour. Also, a committee could have delved into the difficulties which still face agriculture, and might have drawn up a programme commensurate with the needs of our agricultural people. And these committees should recommend legislation to write on the statute books of this country what is necessary to ensure a permanent foundation which will stand us in good stead when the days of peace follow.
Our ability to go on after this war to security, to social and economic reestablish-
Post-War Reconstruction

ment, depends to a large degree upon what we as a nation accomplish now. The foundations of our national life must be laid now if the future is to have stability. Those of us who look back over this last period of years, know that the world is moving with great rapidity, moving over a course which I hope it will never have to re-travel. To be realistic we must acknowledge that as a nation we shall emerge from this conflict as a strong capitalist state; yet I would dare to say that as such we shall emerge from this war very much different from the nation we were in 1939.
To win this war the government has seen fit to impose upon private enterprise certain controls, and for the time being private enterprise has seen fit, on account of war emergency, to accept those controls. The question which faces any committee on post-war reconstruction is one of the degree of control which shall be considered necessary in the future. The question which comes before any committee of this kind is, whether in the general interests of the nation these mild controls necessary to our war-time endeavour shall continue so that it shall be possible to raise the levels of living and security for all our people, or whether private enterprise and corporate interests in Canada will be strong enough after the winning of this war to turn back the clock, to destroy all we have built during these years of war for national unity. If they do that there will be, according to all the laws of economics, but one course for us to follow-the road backward, a road upon which we shall travel toward an era of wide and unrestricted competition, resulting in another period of chaos such as we went through in the 'thirties.
A committee on reconstruction has to consider this question of controls before it can embark upon any ideas of spacious living for the future. In my opinion one of the greatest bulwarks of strength upon which we' can rely as a nation is the determinations set forth by the Atlantic charter and the hope that we have with the other united nations of collaboration with them in the post-war period to bring not only cultural but economic and social advancement to the peoples of all the united nations. In a post-war reconstruction era we, as a nation, must strive for the maximum of peaceful orderly development. That, Mr. Speaker, is the goal for which we must strive. During the war the government of this country has not been afraid to embark upon new ways of doing things. It has not been afraid to try new measures. We face, after this war is over, a new world with new

conditions, conditions greatly of our own making. We must not then cling to old ways just because they are familiar to us. In times of reconstruction after the war this government must face problems in as realistic a manner as it has done in the war period and not be averse to trying new ways and new things to do.
Canada, of course, was the first nation to try price control for the curbing of inflation and did so with a great measure of success. It will be a wonderful thing in the history of these coming years if the government of Canada could be one of the first to introduce new controls to ensure the gainful employment of her own people as the first requisite for post-war reconstruction. Ways can be found.
The Atlantic charter which pledges to the peoples of the united nations continued cooperation and collaboration between them was born of war emergency. In my opinion the future trade and peace relations of this nation with others depend upon the continuation of collaboration and cooperation between the united nations. Any proposals brought forward by the committee on reconstruction must be built upon the realistic and solid implementation of the Atlantic charter and all that it stands for.
I would say again, Mr. Speaker, that whatever is brought forward by way of suggestions for post-war reconstruction by the committee must be made known at the earliest possible moment to the Canadian people. I am one of those who believe that no proposals of any committee can have life and health in them unless they have the will and the cooperation of the people of this nation behind them. For this reason I would advocate that any suggestions of this committee be brought before the people of Canada so that wide public discussion may take place upon the issues which face us. Only in that way can recommendations from the various groups in this country be brought before the committee and be embodied in its proposals.
I wonder if the majority of the people today realize how much of our thinking in pre-war days was dominated by the propaganda of our enemy. One of the great aims of Hitler during the pre-war years was to foist upon the people of the world the lie that the peoples of the Union of the Soviet Socialist Republics and their leaders were the enemy of the people of the world. To the degree that it was possible Hitler endeavoured to isolate the people of the U.S.S.R. from the rest of the world, and to a great degree he was successful. But it would be too bad if, after the

Post-War Reconstruction
experience of these war years, we, as a nation, were to slip back into some of our pre-war thinking. It would be too bad if, after winning the military victory which we all believe will be possible for us, we should allow Hitler to win an ideological victory by continuing to destroy the faith and the confidence which have been established among the united nations during the war.
To-day the people of the U.S.S.R. and the people of Britain have a pact of collective security for the maintenance of peaceful relations for twenty years into the future. I hope very much that this nation will adhere to that pact and do everything possible to make it become a reality. To my mind it is one of the greatest guarantees for the advancement of social and economic progress in this country and all the other countries working with us.
I should like to suggest that this committee on reconstruction beware of the outcry which is likely to be raised from certain elements within this country and perhaps elsewhere against all measures of reform which will be labelled as socialist or red in their content. A situation already exists and is possibly known to members of this house where disruptive elements are tending to destroy the confidence which the united nations have between each other. Editorials are already appearing in our newspapers trying to bring to the forefront of the minds of our people fear and apprehensions as to what will be done by the U.S.S.R. after the war is over, as to what she will desire to have as her share of war spoils and what she will try to dictate in the post-war world. Such slanderous attacks as these must be guarded against and against them such a committee as we are setting up must be warned. Not only that, but within the very boundaries of this nation slanderous attacks are already being made upon labour and upon people's organizations. These are being made by the voices of appeasement which in years gone by strove to cause disunity among us and to spell defeat before we had even attempted to gather our forces and fight. They will now try to turn the clock back by labelling every reform as revolutionary. We must guard against this and see to it that every reform which is possible within the boundaries of a capitalist nation is brought forward for the people of this country who are planning and working for it. The voices of appeasement must be stilled, now and forever.
A marvellous opportunity lies before the people of Canada. We can emerge from this war stronger; we can rise as a nation to
greater heights than we have ever reached before, remembering, of course, always that the true prosperity of a nation must be judged by the living standards of its people. Their education, their culture, their health, their security and the political and economic freedom which they enjoy-those are the things and those alone which spell the greatness of a nation. It is not the profits of its industry, it is not the assets of its banks, which spell the prosperity and greatness of a nation.
The committee must see to it that those new Canadians who are born to us in the coming years are born into homes where they are greeted with happy expectancy. Members of this committee must see to it that the children of this nation are regarded by our people as its most cherished and precious possession. They must see to it that the children of all our people have an equal opportunity to develop their talent and use it for the national good. They must see to it that our young people are happy in the knowledge that society has a place for them and for their creative efforts. And they must see to it that all our people have the assurance of security to establish homes and have children as is their natural right. Our returned men and women must be made to feel the tangible and concrete gratitude of this nation; the maimed and the sick and the blind and the aged and the widowed must be cared for and live as honoured citizens.
These things can be done by a nation which has the will to do them. The poet Browning has said that a man's reach should exceed his grasp. In the matter of reconstruction I say, let us reach out for the stars. Nothing short of that must satisfy us. Let us build a Canada, not where selfish interests are allowed to work for "me and mine," but one in which all the people of Canada walk forward together as one nation, confident that they are working for "us and ours".
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): With the stirring review of the nation's finances by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) ringing in our ears, I scarcely think it would be fair to the house, and possibly not fair to myself, that I should indulge at this time in any extended or comprehensive review of this debate. I rose for one purpose, namely to extend my own thanks to the members of the house, and especially to the hon. members who took part in this debate, for some of the most constructive contributions that I have heard during twenty-three years of parliamentary life. There was hardly a partisan note or tinge in
Post-War Reconstruction

the whole debate. I am sure that what was said here will be of immeasurable benefit to the committee when it is constituted.
Just a word to recall the history of these various committees. On December 2, 1939, or only about a month after the war broke out, the first cabinet committee on demobilization and rehabilitation was formed. Shortly afterwards, in February, 1941, the terms of reference of that committee were extended to appoint a committee on reconstruction, and the actual personnel of that committee was formed on September 2, 1941. As a result of the formation of the cabinet committee there was appointed a general advisory committee on demobilization and rehabilitation, and that committee with ten subcommittees has been very largely responsible for all the work that has been done in the last two or three years in preparing for the reestablishment of our fighting men, when they return. Someone said last night, unknowingly, that very little had been done in three years. I wonder if that hon. member had forgotten that the pensions committee sat in this house in 1941 and that as a result of their deliberations there was enacted by this parliament what I believe to be with all its flaws-there are some flaws-the finest piece of pension legislation in any country in the world to-day.
Last year there were passed in this house three pieces of legislation-and not by order in council: the Vocational Training Coordination Act, the Compulsory Reinstatement Act, and as a result of eighteen months' deliberation by one of these committees, the Veterans' Land Act, which I think is one of the finest acts that we have on the statute books of Canada. Although the work of many of these committees has been temporarily concluded, we are still working on the question of priorities in demobilization, still working on the question of an improved scheme of returned soldiers' allowances, and administration is being improved as fast as we can from day to day. That is touching on the angle of reestablishment.
Touching on the angle of reconstruction I wish to pay my tribute to the excellent work done by those six distinguished Canadians who not only have been studying with about one hundred assistants and consultants all the problems of our national economy in Canada, but have touched upon every single problem that has been mentioned in this debate: soil erosion; rural electrification; the Ganaraska watershed, and other waters in Manitoba and flowing into the St. Lawrence and all over Canada; agriculture, with the cooperation and excellent advice of my distinguished colleague

the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); mines and resources with the assistance of my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar); public works under the direction of the chief engineer of the Department of Public Works; employment boards under the distinguished leadership of Mr. Tom Moore, whose services unfortunately we -were not able to retain for the last few months, but we have another excellent gentleman from Vancouver whom I know well, Mr. Percy Bengough, who will carry on and do all he can to see that labour is protected. Someone on the opposite side said the other evening that labour might be forgotten. Labour will have its proper and adequate representation. So will agriculture. We are trying to represent the interests of all the people of Canada. That work is going on. We now have a subcommittee of the economic advisory committee coordinating the efforts of the various committees, and they are all reporting to my distinguished and right hon. leader the president of the privy council of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). Thus it will be seen that we have now a coordinated effort in regard to the problems of reconstruction.
Reconstruction is not the same as social security. Reconstruction is the positive side of the question. Reconstruction is a challenge to government to develop positive policies, to ensure that gainful employment, or if you like, optimum employment, is available for those who are able and willing to work. Social security comes in only for the very young or the very old or those who are sick or hurt or maimed or invalided. That is a challenge to government; and that is why the Beveridge report, brilliant and able as it is, is no complete solution to the problems of the nation. The Beveridge report comes only in as a safeguard of social security when positive measures of reconstruction have to a certain extent failed. Complete cooperation between both reconstruction and social security policies is requisite, and that is what the government is now seeking to obtain through the efforts of committees of this parliament-and they are supreme over any committees outside. Their recommendations will have a tremendous influence with the government. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) asked the other evening as to the status of this committee.
I say that when this committee makes recommendations to the government they will receive the most earnest and careful attention of the government. This committee on reconstruction will do exactly what the pensions

Railways and Shipping
committee did two years ago; it will call in officials of the reconstruction committee, officials of the economic advisory committee, people from other parts of Canada and outside, from the provinces if you like, and will make careful recommendations to the government. The government will be then possessed of the facts and will determine its policies. It is ridiculous to ask any government at the present time to declare policies in regard to reconstruction. All any government can do at this stage is to have ideals and objectives, and that I think we all have in this house.
Free enterprise was condemned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and commended by others. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid my position is halfway between the two schools of thought. I think free enterprise has gone in the history of this world. I think controlled enterprise must be the guiding maxim for future governments of mankind. We must never let capital run rampant again, and we must never again have the exploitation of natural and human resources that we sometimes had in days gone by. Therefore this is a programme of preparedness.
Once again I thank the house for the support it has given this resolution, and I thank hon. members for the kindly comments which many of them were good enough to extend to its sponsor.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
I think before this committee is appointed the minister should say a word as to the procedure which will be followed. When this committee was first appointed, in the days of the late Mr. Graham, who took a great deal of interest in this work, it was made a rule that any private member of the house interested in the rialway question could attend the meetings of the committee and ask questions. That practice was followed for four or five years. I understand, however, that this rule has now been abrogated, with the result that members of this house have little opportunity of offering suggestions or constructive criticism in connection with our great public utility. We are at present conducting a war. From the beginning of the war to the end of 1940, according to a return tabled for me they received from the government for war work for 16 months, a period of a year and four months, the Canadian Pacific Railway $2,750,000, and the Canadian National $2,500,000, or more than they received in the four years of the last war. With all due respect I contend that this committee should consider suggestions and even resolutions presented by private members. For instance, I believe the government would be well advised to consider whether soldiers cannot be given better treatment. The transport officer issued an order cutting down certain train services during February, which order I understand is to be extended to cover this month as well. No doubt that is quite proper in view of the heavy winter we have experienced, but why should extra trains be provided at week-ends for civilians and not for soldiers? I understand that some of our boys in Camp Borden have not left that camp since Christmas. Many of those soldiers are family men. I know of one whose wife had a child the other day, and he was not able to be with her.
Then I think there should be some provision for considering special cases of soldiers. For example, many of the trains I have seen occupied by soldiers, at Brockville and many other points, are most unsatisfactory. But while soldiers are prohibited from travelling, we see in the newspapers almost every other day where some young Canadian athlete is
Railways and Shipping

transferred from Hamilton to Victoria to take part in games; then he shows up back in Hamilton again, and finally he goes to Halifax. During all this time the soldiers are not allowed to travel at all.
I do not wish to hold up this resolution at any length, but this public utility has cost the taxpayers of Canada a great deal of money and we are never given an opportunity to discuss the affairs of this system except perhaps two or three days before the session closes, when we may have an hour or so devoted to the committee's report. In view of all the money the railways are making I think the public are entitled to some reduction in fares. Soldiers are not permitted to hitchhike ; they may not go more than fifty miles on a bus, and as a result soldiers going to Camp Borden are dumped off at a point about twelve miles from Barrie and left to cover the remainder of the distance as best they can. I think the railways should be able to afford to carry soldiers and their families free over weekends. As it is now, it costs a soldier $2.25 to go home to Toronto from Camp Borden for a weekend, and if he wants to visit his family during his last leave it takes almost a week's pay. Then what is the government going to do about this Almonte disaster? Have we two bodies regulating our railways-the railway commission and the transport officer? What are the functions of these bodies?
Then there is the merchant marine, and I think we should do something about that. We have boats running from Toronto to Port Dalhousie, and one of those boats is not suitable at all. I am afraid something will happen to it, because it has been on the lake for many yeafs. It was not good enough for Northumberland strait and therefore they sent it to the run between Port Dalhousie and Toronto, while they provided a large car ferry for Northumberland strait. I do not object to that; we were glad to see them get it, but apparently any old boat is good enough for lake Ontario. It is a wonder there has not been an accident before this, and newspaper articles show that there have been close calls. I contend that not enough information about this system is given to the public, who after all are the trustees, the owners of it. What are we doing about the tourist trade? We never have any opportunity of discussing these matters, and as a supporter of public ownership in this country I urge that the taxpayer, who has paid all these capital charges and who in addition must pay high transportation costs, should be given better service.

Another question is the suburban steam service. Every large city such as New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Baltimore and so on, has a steam suburban service, which has built up the districts surrounding those cities. Let us consider the suburban service the city of Montreal has, and I would point out that under the Railway Act every other municipality is entitled to the same opportunity, upon application to the board of transport commissioners. The fact is, however, that Montreal is about the only city that has that service.
I plead with the minister to give proper consideration to steam suburban service for the larger cities, and I believe, if that service were given, it would do much to relieve the housing situation. Around Toronto we have a system of radials and buses, now owned by the city. Those systems have built up the outlying districts, so that North York, East York and West York are to a great extent inside suburban constituencies. Rural ridings have become urban ridings. When there is money for capital and maintenance of the Canadian National Railways I ask that something be done so that we may have a more modem system to take care of that problem after the war.
I have attended one or two meetings of the committee, and I have been very much disappointed. All the members seemed to be smoking cigars, and there was much humour at times in evidence. One would think he was attending a vaudeville show, because everyone was in such good humour. They would take up this item and that item, but they were given very little information. I have read the daily reports of the committee and all I have to say is that if that is the way in which we are to-investigate public utilities, then we need some other system. The Canadian Pacific Railway would not conduct its affairs without further inquiries.
Another matter which should be considered is that of auditing. Although we have our own auditor general I do not think he has any check at all, because the railways have auditors of their own. Before the committee they present hotel accounts, maintenance accounts, capital accounts, answers and questions, and that is about the end of it. Then, near the close of the session the committee brings its report to the house. I contend that if the committee system is going to be a success-and this is one case in which it has never been successful-it must change its tactics. There is not enough detailed knowledge in what is contained in the report to parliament.

Railways and Shipping
I do not wish to prevent the passage of the motion, but I hope the new minister will consider these matters. I should like to know if private members will be permitted to attend the committee, although they may not be members of it officially.

Mr. Speaker, before the minister replies may I reiterate, by way of emphasis, what has been said by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). There is a great deal of curiosity throughout the country with respect to the delineation of authority between the transit controller and the board of transport commissioners. I rise at this time only to ask the minister to give that matter consideration when he replies, and to indicate just where the power and authority of the transit controller begin and end, and how they affect or fit in with the power and authority of the board of transport commissioners. He might also indicate whether there has so far been any conflict between these two controls.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, we have very little opportunity to discuss matters pertaining to our railways. This is the first one I can recall in some time. I should like to support the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in his request that greater consideration be given to the matter of suburban services. I have repeatedly placed that subject, as it affects the city of Halifax, before the vice-president of the Atlantic region, the general manager of the Atlantic region and the newly appointed Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud). With the prevailing situation in Halifax, from the point of view of a population greatly increased by the large influx of people, a great many are obliged to live in the suburbs. And as a result of the restrictions on bus travel they are finding it exceedingly difficult to get to and from work during weekdays.
I do not wish to make a lengthy speech, but I would urge that the minister give this matter serious consideration. I am glad the hon. member for Broadview has raised it, and I hope the minister will consider the representations placed before him, with a view to seeing if he can do something to improve suburban services in so far as they affect Halifax, with its overcrowded and greatly increased population.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion carries may I assure hon. members who have spoken, and who have claimed the privilege of appearing before the committee that, so far as I am concerned, in so far as the ndes of the house
permit they will be given every opportunity to appear and to make their suggestions. I am sure they will take advantage of the opportunity offered them. I would request the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) to appear before the committee and lay before the officials of the railways and the different transportation companies which come under the purview of the committee any representations they may have. Let them attend every sitting and take part in the discussions. I am sure they will be given every opportunity to voice their views. They will be given a hearing, and we shall be pleased to have their suggestions for the betterment of transportation services in Canada.
At the present time our facilities are limited, not by money or capital but by materials. Those materials are limited through priorities. Our railways-and I speak of the Canadian National Railways, but it is equally true of the Canadian Pacific Railway -are taxed to the limit. They have to transport war materials and great numbers of passengers. We feel that in certain sections and at certain times priority must be given to the transportation of war materials. This necessitates the curtailment of passenger train service, and sacrifices on the part of the travelling public. For the present, until further notice, the policy is that we request the travelling public to travel as little as possible, in order that the movement of war materials and troops may be facilitated.
Second,'our facilities are limited on account of rolling stock. Since the beginning of the war our rolling stock has been taxed to more than capacity, and has been used until it is almost exhausted. We have had to make way for more important war materials, which have priority over railway rolling stock. As a result of this we have not been able to get renewals of rolling stock, as we might have hoped.
Then, may I point out that the auditors of the Canadian National Railways are appointed by act of parliament every year, and it is the duty of parliament to decide whether or not their work is satisfactory. The best way to find out is to appear before the committee when the railway accounts are being considered, and then question railway officials who will be at the disposal of the committee.
With regard to the question asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) as to the different functions and duties of the board of transport commissioners, and the transit controller, may I point out that there are two
Railways and Shipping

officials, namely, the transit controller and the transport controller. The transit controller has nothing to do with transport by railroad, but the transport controller has been appointed as a war official to organize and establish priorities in connection with the transport of different war materials and as between war materials and passenger service. He acts as the controller of war-time transport services, while the board of transport commissioners is a peace-time organization created under the Railway Act. There is no conflict of authority or in the jurisdiction between the two; the one completes the functions of the other.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext: Has the transport controller any authority over any other type of transportation than the railways?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext: No. He attempts to correlate transport as between the railways and the water services.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext: Why would it not be better to leave that under the board of transport commissioners? Why superimpose on the board of transport commissioners another controller? There are enough controllers now without adding another one. You have control now over your railways through the board of transport commissioners. Why could that board not be given the authority given to this controller? They are familiar with the whole business of transportation.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
It is a matter of opinion. There is no conflict of jurisdiction. The transport controller is simply a complement to the board of transport commissioners which is a peace-time organization and which has certain functions to exercise under the Railway Act. The transport controller must exercise extraordinary functions made necessary by war conditions and his duties are established by the War Measures Act. The transport controller has been functioning for some time and his services have been found to be most useful. He has succeeded in establishing some priorities and in bringing about order in the different branches of railroad transportation.
Ever}- opportunity will be given to hon. members to come before the committee in order to obtain information or to make suggestions in connection with the betterment of the transport facilities for goods and people. I hope that when the report of the committee is brought down, valuable suggestions will be made to meet the requirements
fMr. Michaud.]
suggested by the hon. member for Broadview and the senior hon. member for Halifax.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext: Does the transport controller act under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport or of the Department of Munitions and Supply?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext: The transport controller comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport.

That is an additional reason why he should not be there.
Motion (Mr. Michaud) agreed to.
